claims.text: The premelting and melting behavior of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed by stochastic principles established during particle formation.
Inhibiting precursor mobility during particle formation favors formation of a single alloy phase.
Under limited free-atom mobility, increasing the number of atom types makes formation of a random alloy more likely.
The chemical complexity of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles produces varied elemental configurations.
Chemical complexity produces lattice strain in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Chemical complexity produces lattice defects in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Lattice strain induces defects in the nanoparticles.
Lattice strain and defects govern the premelting and melting response of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
The target Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles will form a single-phase high-entropy alloy.
The resulting single-phase Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles will have a strained and defective lattice.
Single-metal Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles have simpler lattice structures and fewer defects than the target high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Entropy-driven formation of high-entropy-alloy materials generally requires high temperatures and controlled cooling rates.
The proposed mechanism is limited to multicomponent high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles synthesized at high temperature with controlled cooling.
Combined in situ X-ray powder diffraction and multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy can resolve phase formation during high-entropy-alloy nanoparticle synthesis.
Changing cooling rate and precursor mobility should alter phase formation, lattice strain, or defect density in the target nanoparticles.
Observation of single-phase particles with minimal lattice strain and defects regardless of synthesis conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
